source: Gopnik & Wellman (2012) Reconstructing constructivism: causal models, Bayesian learning mechanisms and the theory theory
finding: Theory Theory 2.0: children hold abstract causal theories as probabilistic causal graphs and revise them by Bayesian-like learning from evidence and from their own interventions. This gives the old Piaget idea of constructivism a computational account.
numbers: Review of: 2-4 year olds infer structure from covariation (Gopnik 2001); 4-year-olds use backward blocking (Sobel 2004); 4-year-olds rate a block that fired 2 of 3 times as stronger than one that fired 2 of 6 (Kushnir 2005); 4-year-olds carry a conjunctive or disjunctive rule over to new blocks (Lucas).
quote: children can make correct causal inferences from more complex statistical patterns
limits: Written by the theory's authors, so it is a synthesis and not an independent test. Most studies it cites have cells of about 12-25 children from US middle-class samples. Null results are barely mentioned.
agent_relevance: S5 REVISE: treat revision as moving probability between explicit candidate theories after each new observation, not as free rewriting.

source: Gopnik & Wellman (2012) Reconstructing constructivism: causal models, Bayesian learning mechanisms and the theory theory (sampling and variability section)
finding: Children seem to sample hypotheses in proportion to their probability (Denison 2010) instead of always taking the best one. Behaviour inside one age group is very variable, which the authors take as support for sampling-based search.
numbers: Denison et al: 4-year-olds told red or blue chips make a machine go, with 80 red and 20 blue in the bag, answered in about that proportion. Liu et al 2007: of about 50 preschoolers given 20-30 false-belief tasks, 65% passed more than 75% of them, 30% passed fewer than 25%, only 3 were mixed.
limits: Probability matching is also what a noisy associative learner would show. The Denison result is one small study read second hand here.
agent_relevance: Sampling a few hypotheses and revising by elimination is a defensible form of S5. It links to the sampling-and-voting subfield.

source: Gopnik, Sobel, Schulz & Glymour (2001) Causal learning mechanisms in very young children (read second hand via the review and McClelland & Thompson)
finding: 2-, 3- and 4-year-olds used patterns of covariation (screening-off, one-cause, two-cause) to say which blocks are blickets, then chose the right action to make the detector go or stop. Full text was not read.
numbers: Ages 2, 3 and 4. Cell sizes not read this session.
limits: Second hand only (the full-text download failed). The McClelland network fits the same group data, so the data alone do not separate the theories.
agent_relevance: Screening-off (a non-firing object explains away another) is a cheap, checkable operator for S5.

source: McClelland & Thompson (2007) Using domain-general principles to explain children's causal reasoning abilities
finding: A plain connectionist network with no causal module reproduces the blicket results of Gopnik 2001, Sobel 2004 and Sobel and Kirkham. Its answers match probabilities, as children's roughly do. It gets backward blocking only if earlier events are stored and replayed together, not learned one at a time.
numbers: Children say yes to about 67% of stimuli that should not be called blickets in the screening-off and one-cause tasks; the model is cleaner. 4-year-old answers for a block that fired 2 of 3 times lie inside the 95% interval of probability matching.
quote: without appealing to inherent principles or mechanisms specialized for causal as opposed to other forms of reasoning
limits: Fits published group data and was not used to predict new data. The authors admit it needs explicit reconsideration of earlier events, an add-on. Different learners can produce the same group pattern.
agent_relevance: A rival account. If a plain learner gives the same answers, calling the process a theory adds nothing for us. What counts is that earlier evidence is re-read after each new observation.

source: Benton & Rakison (2013) Causal reasoning in infants and adults: revisiting backwards-blocking
finding: Looked for backward blocking in 6-month-olds and adults. Found nothing in infants and no backward-blocking drop in adults on average.
numbers: Exp 1: 19 six-month-olds, habituation. Looking times to the four test events did not differ, F(3,51)=1.55, p=.21. B+ vs B- test events t(5)=0.39, p=.72. Exp 2: 60 adults. Screening-off replicated (rating of A fell, B rose, p<.006). In the backward-blocking trial the rating of B did not drop significantly (t(59)=1.84, p=.07).
limits: Habituation version, not the original child task; a null with 19 infants is weak. The authors say adults split in two: some behave like an associative learner, some like a Bayesian.
agent_relevance: The signature retrospective update is not universal even in adults. Do not assume a model revises items seen earlier unless the operator makes it.

source: Schulz, Gopnik & Glymour (2007) Preschool children learn causal structure from conditional interventions
finding: Four-year-olds used what happened when one gear was removed to decide which gear has the crank and to choose the right causal structure. Three control conditions rule out salience and mere movement.
numbers: 80 children, mean age 4;6. Test condition n=25: 84% right on trial 1, 76% on trial 2, 64% on both (p<.025). Controls n=18 each: movement 56% and 61% (33% on both), still 50% and 28% (6% on both), contrast 61% and 44%, all ns. Exp 2 and 3: 71% (n=14) and 86% (n=14) chose the right structure. Exp 4 (predict evidence from structure): 44-50% right per trial, n=16, only 12% right on all four trials.
quote: Other theories of causal learning do not account for these results.
limits: Small cells; binomial tests against chance only; no head-to-head against an associative learner. Predicting the evidence from a known structure was clearly harder than inferring structure from evidence.
agent_relevance: Intervention-based revision works in preschoolers, but running the forward prediction from the revised model is the weaker half. Let code derive the predictions of a revised theory (G3).

source: Sobel, Yoachim, Gopnik, Meltzoff & Blumenthal (2007) The blicket within: preschoolers' inferences about insides and causes
finding: Four-year-olds link hidden internal parts to causal power: they tracked which inside works and inferred a property from the inside. Three-year-olds leaned on outside appearance.
numbers: Exp 1 (N=64): 61% put the block with the working inside on the detector, one-tailed p=.05; two-tailed p<.10, not significant; strong side bias, chi2(1)=28.90. 83% named the right insert, p<.001. Exp 2 (N=24): chose the internally similar object on about 66% of trials; 58.3% were consistent against 31.25% expected, p=.005. Exp 3 (n=16): about 66% of trials.
limits: The headline Exp 1 result rested on a one-tailed test and was not significant two-tailed. Small samples throughout.
agent_relevance: A reminder that single small child studies are hints. Our G3 rule (test on something not fitted) covers the same risk.

source: Weisberg, Choi & Sobel (2020) Of blickets, butterflies and baby dinosaurs: children's diagnostic reasoning across domains
finding: Large replication of an interactive blicket task with several uncertain causes: children under about 7 are at chance on diagnosing which causes work; only the oldest group (8-10) beats chance. The age pattern carries over to a matched butterfly task but vanishes in a category task about baby dinosaurs.
numbers: Exp 1 N=242, ages 4-10. Proportion correct, blicket: 38.5% (n=39, mean 59 months), 41.0% (n=39, 85 months), 55.3% (n=38, 108 months); butterfly: 26.2% (n=42), 38.1% (n=42), 59.5% (n=42). Chance 33%; only the oldest third beat it (p=.007 blicket, p<.001 butterfly). Exp 2 (N=112) replicated. Exp 3 (N=110): 27% correct on the dinosaur version, not above chance (p=.20).
quote: children might have the basic capacity for diagnostic inference at relatively early ages
limits: Four uncertain causes is harder than the classic two-block task. The dinosaur version changes content as well as surface, so some of the drop is a content effect.
agent_relevance: Boundary on 'child as scientist': real for simple structures, not for diagnosing many uncertain causes at once. Break a many-cause diagnosis into single-cause tests and combine afterwards.

source: Gopnik et al. (2017) Changes in cognitive flexibility and hypothesis search across human life history from childhood to adolescence to adulthood
finding: In the physical blicket task with an unusual conjunctive rule, willingness to adopt the unusual hypothesis falls with age: 4-year-olds most, then school-age children, adolescents and adults least. Older learners lean on prior beliefs over evidence.
numbers: Exp 1 new data: 6-7 year olds n=90, 9-11 n=90, 12-14 n=86, joined to the 4-year-olds and adults of Lucas 2014. Share calling the key object D a blicket under the conjunctive rule: 4-year-olds 0.92; 6-7 0.56 (P<.01 vs 4); 9-11 0.60; 12-14 0.28 (P<.05 vs younger); adults 0.25. Overall conjunctive 0.52 vs disjunctive 0.13 and baseline 0.15. Using several objects to start the machine: 4-year-olds 0.84 vs 6-7 0.53 (P<.05). Exp 2 added 240 online adults for a social task; preschoolers and adolescents were most flexible there.
limits: Procedures differ somewhat across ages (adults online). The social domain does not show one age curve. Adults' behaviour may reflect a sensible prior, not a deficit.
agent_relevance: A learner with strong priors under-revises when the evidence points to an unusual rule. Widen the candidate list with unlikely hypotheses before updating.

source: Lucas, Bridgers, Griffiths & Gopnik (2014) When children are better (or at least more open-minded) learners than adults
finding: Preschoolers generalised an unusual conjunctive causal rule to new objects more often than adults, who kept a disjunctive default. A Bayesian model with a flexible prior fits the children.
numbers: Not read in full. Counts for 4-year-olds vs adults appear through Gopnik 2017 (0.92 vs 0.25 for the key object under the conjunctive rule).
limits: Abstract and secondary sources only. Sample sizes not read.
agent_relevance: Source of the 'conjunctive handicap' that the 2025-2026 LLM papers test.

source: Bonawitz, Shafto, Gweon, Goodman, Spelke & Schulz (2011) The double-edged sword of pedagogy: instruction limits spontaneous exploration and discovery
finding: After a teacher shows one function of a toy, preschoolers explore less and find fewer other functions. A teacher's silence about other functions is read as evidence they do not exist.
numbers: Exp 1: 25 children pedagogical, 20 each in three other conditions. Play time 119.2 s vs 179.6 (interrupted), 132.7 (naive), 205.7 (baseline), F(1,81)=4.52, p<.05. Kinds of action 4.00 vs 5.30, 5.90, 6.15, p<.01. Other target functions found 0.72 vs 1.3, 1.2, 1.15, p<.05. Share of play on the shown squeaker 0.68 vs 0.53 and 0.38. Exp 2 (64 preschoolers): narrowing after instruction to self or to another child, not after instruction to an adult.
limits: Naive-condition play time was also short, so tiredness is not fully excluded. One lab. The effect depends on who counts as the teacher.
agent_relevance: A prompt that shows one worked solution can stop the model from looking for others. Keep several candidates in view in the revision prompt.

source: Kosoy et al. (2022) Learning causal overhypotheses through exploration in children and computational models (CLeaR)
finding: Children aged 4-5 explored a blicket machine much better when told which kinds of rule were possible. They explored the same amount whether the rule was OR or AND, and always took more steps than information-gain agents.
numbers: N=85 children aged 4-5 (20-23 per condition). Share who produced enough data to settle the rule: 71% with the hypothesis space given vs 32% without (2-proportion test p=.002). Actions 14.07 vs 10.58; time 178.65 s vs 195.38 s. About 17.7% and 17.5% tested the empty machine. The information-gain agents always generated enough data.
limits: Museum sample. Children being efficient depends on being given the space of options; they are not optimal.
agent_relevance: State the family of possible rules before the model proposes a test; that is what raised information quality here.

source: Kosoy, Chan, Liu, Collins, Kaufmann, Huang, Hamrick, Canny, Ke & Gopnik (2022) Towards understanding how machines can learn causal overhypotheses
finding: In a blicket benchmark, RL and imitation agents learn the AND-or-OR overhypothesis slowly or not at all. GPT-3 and PaLM named the causal structure well when it was given but often named the wrong objects.
numbers: Decision Transformer forced-choice accuracy on structure: 0.67 (random data), 0.71, 0.73, 0.77 with 5, 10, 15 forced exploration steps; reward 0.16 vs 2.37 (15 steps). Behaviour cloning 0.55-0.68. GPT-3 and PaLM: 1-8 trials per condition; GPT-3 named too many objects as blickets; chain-of-thought did not help PaLM.
limits: Language-model part is tiny and descriptive (text-davinci-002, PaLM) with no statistics. Old models.
agent_relevance: Forced exploration before acting raised structure accuracy; supports an explicit explore-then-conclude gate.

source: Yiu, Kosoy & Gopnik (2023) Imitation versus innovation: what children can do that large language and language-and-vision models cannot (yet)
finding: Models match children and adults when picking the object that goes with a typical tool, but fall behind when they must pick a superficially different object with the right causal function. Models also struggled to learn novel causal structure from blicket data.
numbers: Children aged 3-7 (n=42) and adults (n=30): superficial match 88.4% and 84.9%; function-based innovation 85.2% and 95.7%. Models (six option orders, temperature 0): innovation GPT-4 75.9%, gpt-3.5-turbo 58.9%, Claude 58.2%, Flan 45.7%, davinci 8.9%; imitation GPT-4 83.3%, gpt-3.5 73.1%, Claude 69.9%, Flan 74.8%, davinci 59.9%.
limits: Models of 2023. Once a test is described online later models may have seen it. Why GPT-4 did better (images or feedback training) is unknown.
agent_relevance: Choose by causal function, not by association; old models lean on nearest-neighbour association. Test this in S5.

source: Yiu, Kosoy & Gopnik (2024) Transmission versus truth, imitation versus innovation (Perspectives on Psychological Science)
finding: Published version: language models are good at interpolating cultural knowledge and weaker at discovering new causal truths by acting on the world.
numbers: Same figures as the preprint (GPT-4 75.9% innovation vs adults 95.7%; imitation GPT-4 83.3%).
limits: Argument paper. It does not test current reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Frames the gap our scaffold must close: knowledge inside the model versus evidence gathered by acting. That needs run checks, not more thinking.

source: GX-Chen, Lin, Samiei, Precup et al. (2025) Language agents mirror human causal reasoning biases. How can we help them think like scientists? (COLM 2025)
finding: Language models find disjunctive (OR) blicket rules but fail conjunctive (AND) ones, even given oracle exploration data. The disjunctive bias is adult-like, not child-like. A test-time method that samples many hypotheses and then eliminates them removes the bias.
numbers: Models: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-chat, DeepSeek-reasoner, QwQ, Gemma3, Llama. The information-gain oracle gets 1.0 every time; models drop from 4 to 8 objects and from OR to AND. With oracle exploration data only DeepSeek-reasoner came near perfect. Hypothesis sampling with 16, 32, 64, 96 initial unique hypotheses: accuracy rose with more samples and the AND-OR gap went away.
limits: Per-model accuracies are mostly in figures. Text task with only OR and AND rules. Human data are borrowed from Gopnik 2017.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G1 and S5: the fix that worked was a code-driven sample-then-eliminate loop, not longer reasoning. The bias is present in current models.

source: GX-Chen et al. (2025) correlates of success and exploration profile
finding: Information gained by the tests tracks success; length of reasoning does not. In a child-style 3-object setup, models spend less time exploring OR rules, unlike children (Kosoy 2022).
numbers: Spearman correlation with all-correct accuracy (8 objects): information gain 0.76; unique states visited 0.33 (p<0.05); steps before exit -0.35; response length -0.30. Children (4-year-olds) infer an AND machine when the evidence says so; models lean OR even with AND hints.
limits: Correlations over model-prompt-rule combinations, not over trials. Human data from earlier papers.
agent_relevance: Use code-computed information gain of each test as the S5 progress monitor; do not use length of reasoning.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky & Choi (2026) Failing to falsify: evaluating and mitigating confirmation bias in language models
finding: Eleven LLMs show confirmation bias in a Wason rule-discovery game: they propose tests that fit their current guess. A prompt borrowed from human work (think in opposites) lowers the bias and lifts discovery. Distilling that behaviour transfers partly to the blicket test.
numbers: Task success from 6% to 78% across 11 models in 45 turns. Counterexample prompting raised rule discovery from 42% to 56% on average. Blicket task, Qwen3-8B: success 0.32 base vs 0.40 with think-in-opposites (test ratio 0.44 vs 0.57); Qwen3-32B: 0.57 vs 0.86 (ratio 0.54 vs 1.31). Models distilled on the Wason task: 8B student 0.34 and 0.36 success. A higher incompatible-to-compatible test ratio goes with higher success.
limits: Gains are significant for thinking models, small or mixed for non-thinking ones. Distillation transfers less than task-specific prompting. Table values are from text extraction with some scrambled columns.
agent_relevance: After a revised theory is proposed, force at least one test chosen to fail it, selected by code (a G3-style falsifier).

source: Samiei, Yiu, GX-Chen, Lin, Shen, Richards, Gopnik & Precup (2026) Human adults and LLMs as scientists: who benefits from active exploration?
finding: Adults' known trouble with AND rules goes away when they choose their own tests. Planning tests is not enough: you must see the outcomes of your own tests. Strong LLMs match top humans on OR rules but most fall behind on AND rules.
numbers: 306 Prolific adults, 102 per group (active, passive observer, passive proposer). Conjunctive object identification: active 0.69, passive observer 0.45, passive proposer 0.12. Rule choice: 0.82, 0.69, 0.57. GPT-5 and DeepSeek-reasoner match top humans on OR. Many models fall far on AND; deepseek-chat and o4-mini are only modestly above a random baseline.
limits: June 2026 preprint, not peer reviewed. New 'nexiom' text task, adults only; no child group.
agent_relevance: Revision works when the agent runs its own test and sees the result (G2). The step that picks the test must also receive its outcome.

source: Alderete, Benthall, Xu & Xing (2026) Separable pathways for causal reasoning: how architectural scaffolding enables hypothesis-space restructuring in LLM agents
finding: A blicket scaffold that detects when the current hypothesis space is wrong and widens it. Two parts do different jobs: a state-graph structure improves reasoning inside the new space, a monitor triggers the switch. All agents used Claude Sonnet 4.5 (Haiku 4.5 for the trigger).
numbers: 1,085 trials. Pooled raw accuracy: base 87.3% (96/110), graph 77.3% (85/110), graph plus monitor 89.1% (98/110). Graph plus monitor beat graph alone, Fisher one-tailed p=.015. Run 03 (n=30 each): base 76.7%, graph 76.7%, both 93.3%. The graph drove 94% of the gain in post-switch reasoning accuracy. Monitor sensitivity 100% across five datasets. Cost 30-50% above base. A hidden-moderator run: +10pp, p=.276, not significant.
limits: One model family, one company lab, preprint. The graph alone was numerically worse than base on raw accuracy (not significant). Ceiling effects in several runs.
agent_relevance: Closest published match to our S5, yet the net gain over the plain model was small (87.3% to 89.1%) at a 30-50% cost, so G7 applies.

source: Alderete et al. (2026) exactly-N trap and decomposition
finding: Raw accuracy hides a structural trap: all agents score 0% on the 'exactly-N' category regardless of architecture, and 100% before the rule switch. The graph's raw loss came from more exposure to that trap, not worse reasoning.
numbers: Exposure to the trap: base 10.9%, graph 21.8%, graph plus monitor 9.1%. Reasoning accuracy: graph 98.7% vs base 97.5%.
limits: The trap explanation is the authors' post hoc account.
agent_relevance: When comparing arms at equal tokens (G7), split the score by case type or a hidden category effect decides the winner.

source: Weisberg, Choi & Sobel (2020) design check and age model
finding: Within-subject Exp 2 (N=112) reproduced the age curve and showed no sex or order effects. The dinosaur task showed no reliable age effect, and overall accuracy stayed at chance.
numbers: Exp 2 age effect Wald chi2=19.86, p<0.001. Exp 3: 27% correct overall, binomial p=0.20; age model p=0.08, not significant.
limits: Dinosaur task asks about category membership, not a causal system, so it differs in content and structure.
agent_relevance: Tests of transfer must change the story; a scaffold that passes one story may fail a parallel one.

source: Gopnik & Wellman (2012) on exploration (Schulz & Bonawitz 2007; Cook, Goodman & Schulz 2011), second hand
finding: Preschoolers play more with a toy whose causal structure was left confounded than with one demonstrated clearly. The review reads this as theory-driven information seeking.
numbers: Described design only: a two-lever toy, confounded vs unconfounded demonstration. No counts in the review; original papers not read.
limits: Original papers not opened. A novelty or boredom reading of more play at an unresolved toy is not ruled out in the review.
agent_relevance: An unresolved confound is a good trigger for more exploring (fits G1: explore on a signal).

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) intervention effects across models
finding: Think-in-Opposites improves task success in every model listed in the Wason table, and both interventions raise the ratio of disconfirming to confirming tests in most cases. The shift is clear in thinking-mode models and not in non-thinking models.
numbers: Both interventions raised the incompatible-to-compatible ratio in 18 of 22 model-variant cases. Qwen3-8B Wason: thinking baseline success 0.21, rising to 0.40 with think-in-opposites. Non-thinking Qwen3-8B stayed at 0.06 with it.
limits: Small open models; permutation tests; no human baseline in the same task.
agent_relevance: The falsification step helps only if the model can use extra reasoning; check this on the model we deploy before adding it (G7).

source: Kosoy et al. (2022) children's identification accuracy by rule
finding: Children's accuracy at naming blickets differed little between OR and AND machines, except the OR condition with the hypothesis space given, where they did much better. This agrees with Lucas 2014.
numbers: Group differences were p<0.02 except between the two AND given-hypothesis conditions; 66.7% and 65% of children tried different orderings of the same objects in the two hypothesis conditions.
limits: Reported as figures; exact true and false positive rates not read as numbers.
agent_relevance: Children are not biased toward OR when they act and watch; the LLM bias is therefore a model property, not a task property.

source: Gopnik & Wellman (2012) on infants (second hand) versus Benton & Rakison (2013)
finding: The review cites 18-month-olds (Sobel & Kirkham 2007) and 16-month-olds (Gweon & Schulz 2011) as showing causal inference from covariation. Benton & Rakison, with 19 six-month-olds, found no sign of backward blocking and called the earlier infant evidence mixed.
numbers: No new numbers; 16- and 18-month claims against a null with 19 infants.
limits: Looking-time studies are hard to interpret and the two labs did not test the same age or task.
agent_relevance: Treat infant Bayes claims as unsettled and build nothing on them.
